"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
There are just four weeks to go until election day.
More than a million people have already cast their ballots, and more than a billion dollars
in political ads are planned across key House and Senate contests.
NPR's Stephen Fowler has this look at the political landscape.
The map of races both parties view as competitive is expansive and runs deep into states where
President Trump comfortably won in 2024.
And the House party committees have ID'd close to 100 seats, they feel are in play, with
millions in spending lined up to try and shape the outcome.
And in the Senate, Republicans have pulled back money from Georgia and North Carolina,
where Democrats are pulling better, instead sending resources to places like Kansas and
South Carolina, where Trump's unpopularity makes the midterm more competitive than one
might expect.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
The Trump administration is urging Russia to be more transparent about the death of a lab
worker in Siberia last week in a suspected case of pneumatic plague.
NPR's Michelle Kellerman reports that the State Department says it's been in touch with
Russia's foreign ministry since last Friday, when the news first emerged.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio sounded frustrated with the lack of information, but he wouldn't
speculate when asked whether this could have been a leak of a strain of the plague that
was altered by Russia.
I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world.
That's what they should do.
That's what we hope they will do.
And the more we can learn about what happened, then the better all of us can be in a position
of responding.
So far, it is State Department health experts who have been reaching out to Russia for information,
though arms control experts have expressed concern that Russia maintains an offensive
biological warfare program.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
Hollywood has a new powerhouse, Paramount's parent company Skydance has formally acquired
Warner Brothers Discovery, NPR's Mondalee Del Barco reports on what this means for major
assets in entertainment, news and the people they employ.
David Ellison is growing his media empire with what will now be known collectively as
Skydance, which he secured for more than $111 billion.
The company merges two legendary movie studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Brothers Pictures.
Skydance also combines their streaming services, cable channels and news outlets CNN and CBS
News.
The mega deal faced protests from actors, writers and others worried about the concentration
of power and political interference, but it ultimately passed legal and regulatory challenges
in the U.S. and abroad.
Ellison is starting out with a huge debt and those who fought to block the merger worry
there will be job cuts.
Mondalee Del Barco, NPR News, Los Angeles.
The S&P 500 climbed more than half a percent today, topping its record set in August.
This is NPR News.
The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees worked so powerfully
during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting and feared
additional exposures.
That's according to a previously unreleased army study.
ICE leaders were aware of the study's findings before signing the $16.7 million contract
to buy 6,000 pairs of shock gloves.
Dirty Dancing is celebrating its 40th anniversary and a stage version will be on Broadway next
year.
Jeff London reports it's being directed by an actor from the movie.
Bonnie Price, who played the role of Neil Kellerman in the original film, is directing
this adaptation.
With a script by screenwriter Eleanor Bergstein, the show will feature songs from the movie,
including this Academy and Grammy Award winner.
The production is part of a North American tour, playing Detroit, Boston and Toronto,
among other cities, before it makes a seven-month stop on Broadway.
Once the show closes in New York next September, it will go back on the road.
For NPR News, I'm Jeff London in New York.

Line judge Jeff Seaman received a two-game suspension for swearing at Arizona tight end
Trey McBride.
